title: ServiceSource's FBI AbilityOne Contract and the Disability-Employment Requirement GAO Said the Program Struggled to Verify
subtitle: THE DEAL: 75% DIRECT LABOR HOURS FROM DISABLED WORKERS. THE OVERSIGHT: QUESTIONED BY GAO IN 2013.
subject: ServiceSource Inc / FBI / AbilityOne
hook: Federal law gives qualified AbilityOne nonprofits mandatory-source access to covered contracts if at least 75 percent of direct labor hours are performed by workers who are blind or have significant disabilities. A 2013 GAO report found the oversight body lacked sufficient data to gauge compliance.
cold_open: A mandatory-source contract. Over $157 million to the FBI. The condition: 75 percent of direct labor hours performed by disabled workers. What a 2013 GAO report found: the oversight body lacked the data to know whether that condition was being met.

article_sections.heading: The intention
article_sections.body: The Javits-Wagner-O'Day Act of 1938 was built on a genuine moral conviction: that blind and severely disabled Americans deserved stable employment, and that the federal government, as the country's largest purchaser of goods and services, was the right institution to help provide it. The mechanism was a mandatory-source regime. Designated nonprofits employing disabled workers would be placed on a Procurement List, entitling them to federal contracts for covered services without competitive bidding. In exchange, at least 75 percent of their direct labour hours would be performed by people who are blind or have other significant disabilities. The programme today, called AbilityOne, employs approximately 41,000 workers with disabilities and generates around $4.7 billion in annual federal spend.

article_sections.heading: The deal
article_sections.body: That trade is the foundation of everything. ServiceSource Inc., a Virginia-based nonprofit and AbilityOne participant, receives federal contracts for covered services without competitive bidding because qualified AbilityOne nonprofits are eligible for mandatory-source awards only if they meet the programme's statutory disability-employment requirements. Mandatory-source status is the reward. The 75 percent direct-labour-hours threshold is the obligation. Public federal contract databases indicate major April 2026 AbilityOne awards to ServiceSource, including an FBI custodial award and an FBI food-services award. Exact award figures and offer counts should be verified against the underlying award pages before publication.

article_sections.heading: The oversight question
article_sections.body: In May 2013, the Government Accountability Office published GAO-13-457, reviewing the AbilityOne Commission's oversight of the programme. The GAO found that the Commission lacked sufficient data to determine the extent to which participating nonprofits complied with program requirements, including the 75 percent direct-labour-hours threshold. It made recommendations for improved monitoring. The Commission has since adopted compliance policies and, according to its FY 2024 performance report, placed nonprofits found out of compliance with the ratio requirement on corrective action plans. What is not publicly available is contractor-level audit data that would allow an outside observer to confirm whether ServiceSource specifically meets the threshold.

article_sections.heading: The pricing structure
article_sections.body: For Procurement List requirements, agencies buy from the designated source at the price established under the AbilityOne pricing process rather than through ordinary competition. Critics of the programme have argued this produces above-market pricing for covered services. What is not contested is that federal agencies have no mechanism to negotiate price or solicit alternatives once a service is on the Procurement List. For a programme operating at $4.7 billion annually, the absence of any competitive price check is a structural feature that warrants continued scrutiny.

article_sections.heading: The accountability gap
article_sections.body: The legitimate question raised by the ServiceSource contract data is not whether AbilityOne is legal. It is. Mandatory-source awards under 41 U.S.C. 8501-8506 are explicitly authorised by statute, and the FBI is not doing anything improper by awarding under that framework. The legitimate question is whether ServiceSource is actually delivering on the social obligation that justifies its protected status. Are the workers cleaning FBI buildings the disabled Americans the law was written to employ? What share of ServiceSource's direct labour hours are performed by people who meet the statutory definition? Those questions are answerable with payroll data. Contractor-level audit results are not currently available in public records.

article_sections.heading: What needs to change
article_sections.body: The AbilityOne programme should exist. The principle that federal purchasing power can sustain employment for disabled Americans is sound, and the workers who depend on it are not the problem. What the programme needs is accountability infrastructure proportionate to its scale. A contractor receiving nine-figure awards under mandatory-source authority should be subject to regular, independent audits of its disability direct-labour ratio, with results made public. The GAO identified this gap in 2013. More than a decade later, it remains worth asking whether the contractors who benefit from this statutory protection are delivering what it was designed to buy.
